entry.title: A novel changepoint detection algorithm

link.title: A novel changepoint detection algorithm

entry.content: Note added in version 2 (2026): this paper has been superseded. The probability it computes, that each index is the most recent changepoint, is the run-length posterior of Bayesian online changepoint detection (R. P. Adams and D. J. C. MacKay, arXiv:0710.3742, 2007), which computes it exactly and efficiently; see also P. Fearnhead, Statistics and Computing 16:203-213, 2006. The implementation used for the results in this paper contained errors, so those results should not be relied on. A corrected implementation, tests, and a description of the errors are at https://github.com/AllenDowney/ChangePoint. The rest of the paper is unchanged from version 1. We propose an algorithm for simultaneously detecting and locating changepoints in a time series, and a framework for predicting the distribution of the next point in the series. The kernel of the algorithm is a system of equations that computes, for each index i, the probability that the last (most recent) change point occurred at i. We evaluate this algorithm by applying it to the change point detection problem and comparing it to the generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) algorithm. We find that our algorithm is as good as GLR, or better, over a wide range of scenarios, and that the advantage increases as the signal-to-noise ratio decreases.

entry.title: Using RngStreams for Parallel Random Number Generation in C++ and R

link.title: Using RngStreams for Parallel Random Number Generation in C++ and R

entry.content: The RngStreams software package provides one viable solution to the problem of creating separate random number streams for simulations in parallel processing environments. Techniques are presented for effectively using RngStreams with C++ programs that are parallelized via OpenMP or MPI. Ways to access the backbone generator from RngStreams in R through the parallel and rstream packages are also described. The ideas in the paper are illustrated with both a simple running example and a Monte Carlo integration application.

entry.title: Causal Inference Under Unmeasured Confounding With Negative Controls: A Minimax Learning Approach

link.title: Causal Inference Under Unmeasured Confounding With Negative Controls: A Minimax Learning Approach

entry.content: We study the estimation of causal parameters when not all confounders are observed and instead negative controls are available. Recent work has shown how these can enable identification and efficient estimation via two so-called bridge functions. In this paper, we tackle the primary challenges in causal inference with negative controls: identifying and estimating these bridge functions. Previous work has typically relied on completeness conditions for identification, imposed uniqueness assumptions for estimation, and focused on parametric models for the bridge functions. Instead, we provide an alternative identification strategy that assumes the existence of two bridge functions rather than completeness conditions. We also provide new estimators for these functions based on minimax learning formulations. These estimators accommodate general function classes such as Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces and neural networks. We study finite-sample convergence results both for estimating bridge functions themselves and for the final estimation of the causal parameter under a variety of combinations of assumptions. We avoid uniqueness conditions on the bridge functions as much as possible.

entry.title: A multistate approach to disability insurance reserving with information delays

link.title: A multistate approach to disability insurance reserving with information delays

entry.content: Disability insurance claims are often affected by lengthy reporting delays and adjudication processes. The classic multistate life insurance modeling framework is ill-suited to handle such information delays since the cash flow and available information can no longer be based on the biometric multistate process determining the contractual payments. We propose a new individual reserving model for disability insurance schemes which describes the claim evolution in real-time. Under suitable independence assumptions between the available information and the underlying biometric multistate process, we show that these new reserves may be calculated as natural modifications of the classic reserves. For estimation of the model constituents, we employ the procedure proposed in [Buchardt, K., Furrer, C., & Sandqvist, O. L. (2025). Estimation for multistate models subject to reporting delays and incomplete event adjudication. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 19(4), 2782-2802. https://doi.org/10.1214/25-AOAS2068]. A real data application illustrates how the proposed estimation and reserving methods can be implemented and compares the resulting reserves with simpler reserving approaches.

entry.title: Discovering and Reasoning of Causality in the Hidden World with Large Language Models

link.title: Discovering and Reasoning of Causality in the Hidden World with Large Language Models

entry.content: Revealing hidden causal variables alongside the underlying causal mechanisms is essential to the development of science. Despite the progress in the past decades, existing practice in causal discovery (CD) heavily relies on high-quality measured variables, which are usually given by human experts. In fact, the lack of well-defined high-level variables behind unstructured data has been a longstanding roadblock to a broader real-world application of CD. This procedure can naturally benefit from an automated process that can suggest potential hidden variables in the system. Interestingly, Large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive observations of the world and have demonstrated great capability in processing unstructured data. To leverage the power of LLMs, we develop a new framework termed Causal representatiOn AssistanT (COAT) that incorporates the rich world knowledge of LLMs to propose useful measured variables for CD with respect to high-value target variables on their paired unstructured data. Instead of directly inferring causality with LLMs, COAT constructs feedback from intermediate CD results to LLMs to refine the proposed variables. Given the target variable and the paired unstructured data, we first develop COAT-MB that leverages the predictivity of the proposed variables to iteratively uncover the Markov Blanket of the target variable. Built upon COAT-MB, COAT-PAG further extends to uncover a more complete causal graph, i.e., Partial Ancestral Graph, by iterating over the target variables and actively seeking new high-level variables. Moreover, the reliable CD capabilities of COAT also extend the debiased causal inference to unstructured data by discovering an adjustment set. We establish theoretical guarantees for the CD results and verify their efficiency and reliability across realistic benchmarks and real-world case studies.

entry.title: Transmission Channel Analysis in Dynamic Models

link.title: Transmission Channel Analysis in Dynamic Models

entry.content: We propose a framework for analysing transmission channels in a large class of dynamic models. Our method, labelled Transmission Channel Analysis (TCA), decomposes the total effects captured by impulse response functions into the effects flowing through transmission channels, thereby providing a quantitative assessment of the strength of various well-defined channels. This decomposition requires no identification assumptions beyond those needed to identify the structural shock whose effects the researcher wants to decompose. We provide algorithms to compute the effect through any transmission channel and prove that, for structural vector autoregressive models, impulse response functions are sufficient statistics for doing so. Applications to policy shocks in a variety of popular macroeconomic models demonstrate the empirical relevance of TCA for policy evaluation.

entry.title: Denoising Data with Measurement Error Using a Reproducing Kernel-Based Diffusion Model

link.title: Denoising Data with Measurement Error Using a Reproducing Kernel-Based Diffusion Model

entry.content: Recent advancements in measurement technologies have facilitated the acquisition of high-resolution data in fields such as engineering, biology, and medicine. However, these observations are frequently corrupted by measurement noise. To address this challenge, we propose a denoising framework that employs diffusion models to recover the underlying error-free data distribution, thereby enabling reliable downstream analysis. Central to our framework is a novel Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS)-based method that trains the diffusion model using only error-contaminated data. This method admits a closed-form solution and achieves a fast convergence rate in terms of estimation error. Theoretically, we validate our approach by deriving an upper bound on the total variation distance between the distributions of the generated denoised data and the true error-free data. Extensive simulations demonstrate the superior empirical performance of our method compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Finally, we illustrate the framework’s practical utility in digital health and epidemiology by applying it to Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) data and the association analysis between blood lipids and coronary heart disease.

entry.title: On factors influencing consumer preference in pipeline stages: an experiment

link.title: On factors influencing consumer preference in pipeline stages: an experiment

entry.content: This paper presents a case study on the eClinical data of Intelligent Medical Objects, which currently employs eight pipeline stages. Historically, the pipeline stage progresses inversely with the number of customers. Our objective is to identify the key factors that significantly affect consumer presences at the more advanced stages of the pipeline. Logistic regression is utilized for this analysis. This technique estimates the probability of an event occurring, enabling researchers to evaluate how various factors influence specific outcomes. Widely applied across disciplines such as medicine, finance, and social sciences, logistic regression is particularly useful for classification tasks and identifying the importance of predictors, thus supporting data-driven decision-making. In this study, logistic regression is used to model the likelihood of reaching the eighth pipeline stage as the dependent variable, revealing that only a few independent variables significantly contribute to explaining this outcome.

entry.title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity

link.title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity

entry.content: Treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates is common in instrumental variable (IV) analyses. An intuitive approach, which we call the interacted two-stage least squares (2sls), is to regress the outcome on the treatment, covariates, and treatment-covariate interactions, using the IV, covariates, and IV-covariate interactions as instruments. We clarify the causal interpretation of the interacted 2sls under the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework when the IV is valid conditional on the covariates. Our main findings are twofold. First, we show that the coefficients on the treatment-covariate interactions from the interacted 2sls identify treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates among compliers for any outcome-generating process if and only if the product of the IV propensity score and the covariates is linear in the covariates, a requirement we call the linear IV-covariate interactions condition. Second, when the covariate vector has dimension K and includes a constant term, we show that the linear IV-covariate interactions condition requires the IV propensity score to take at most K distinct values. The condition holds when (a) the covariates take exactly K distinct values, or (b) the IV is randomly assigned independently of the covariates, but is restrictive beyond these cases. These results underscore the difficulty of interpreting regression coefficients from specifications with treatment-covariate interactions when the covariates are not saturated and the IV is not unconditionally randomized, absent correct specification of the outcome model. We then connect these results to the literature on LATE estimation, and show that under the linear IV-covariate interactions condition, the interacted 2sls with covariates demeaned by their complier means recovers the LATE as a single coefficient.

entry.title: Policy Learning with Confidence

link.title: Policy Learning with Confidence

entry.content: This paper introduces a rule for policy selection in the presence of estimation uncertainty, explicitly accounting for estimation risk. The rule belongs to the class of risk-aware rules on the efficient decision frontier, characterized as policies offering maximal estimated welfare for a given level of estimation risk. Among this class, the proposed rule is chosen to provide a reporting guarantee, ensuring that the welfare delivered exceeds a threshold with a pre-specified confidence level. We apply this approach to the allocation of a limited budget among social programs using estimates of their marginal value of public funds and associated standard errors.

entry.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling

link.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling

entry.content: With direct computation of moments through order $L$ in $d$ dimensions, standard method of moments (MM) incurs $\Omega(d^L)$ computation and storage costs, and standard generalized method of moments (GMM) additionally requires estimating and inverting an often ill-conditioned covariance matrix of size $\Omega(d^L)$-by-$\Omega(d^L)$ to obtain the optimal weighting matrix. Pereira, Kileel, and Kolda [arXiv:2202.06930 (2022)] avoid the tensor computation cost of MM through implicit moment computation. Despite this progress, incorporating statistically principled weighting while preserving computational efficiency remains an important challenge, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where sampling variances can differ substantially across moment orders. We introduce diagonally-weighted GMM (DGMM), which assigns one adaptive weight to each moment order through a structured approximation of the optimal weighting matrix while avoiding the covariance inversion, thereby balancing statistical efficiency, computational complexity, and numerical stability. For general parametric models, we prove that DGMM is consistent, asymptotically normal, and near-efficient under explicit structural conditions. For heteroscedastic low-rank Gaussian mixtures, we design a computationally efficient and numerically stable algorithm that extends the implicit moment computation to the DGMM objective, gradients, and weights and incorporates Nystr"om approximations of the kernel sums. In low-SNR experiments with $d=100$ and $L=4$, where standard MM and GMM are infeasible, controlled weighting comparisons show that DGMM achieves consistently small parameter errors across tested initializations, including the challenging starts where alternative weightings struggle, with shorter median runtimes and fewer iterations. The code and data will be available upon publication at https://github.com/liu-lzhang/dgmm.

entry.title: Bayesian Predictive Inference Beyond Martingales

link.title: Bayesian Predictive Inference Beyond Martingales

entry.content: There is growing interest in the so-called Bayesian Predictive Inference approach, which enables Bayesian inference without specifying a likelihood function or prior distribution and without resorting to MCMC methods. Instead, only a sequence of predictive distributions for the observations is required, and inference on the unknown estimand can be performed, cheaply in parallel, using bootstrap-type schemes. Understanding which classes of predictive distributions can be used within this framework, is still a key open question. We relax commonly used probabilistic assumptions on the observations, namely exchangeability and conditionally identical distribution, and on their predictive distributions, which are measure-valued martingales, by introducing the new class of Almost Conditionally Identically Distributed (a.c.i.d.) random variables. This class assumes that the predictive distributions are measure-valued almost supermartingales, and is parametrized by a sequence of parameters $(\xi_{n}){n\geq 0}$, which regulate the decay of conditional dependence among future observations. Under mild summability assumptions on $(\xi{n})_{n\geq 0}$, the resulting sequence of observations is shown to be asymptotically exchangeable, hence amenable to Bayesian Predictive Inference techniques. A.c.i.d. random variables arise naturally in recursive algorithms, and include classic approaches in Statistics and Learning Theory, such as kernel estimators, and more novel ones, such as the parametric Bayesian bootstrap.

entry.title: A-optimal Designs under Generalized Linear Models

link.title: A-optimal Designs under Generalized Linear Models

entry.content: Designing efficient experiments under practical constraints is critical in both scientific research and industrial practice. Focusing on minimizing the average variance of the parameter estimates, A-optimal designs show advantages in screening factors and reducing prediction errors. Compared with other criteria, however, algorithms and software for generating A-optimal designs are scarce. In this paper, we characterize A-optimal designs under generalized linear models theoretically and develop efficient algorithms for identifying them. When a predetermined finite set of experimental settings is given, we derive analytic solutions or establish necessary and sufficient conditions for obtaining A-optimal approximate allocations. We show that a lift-one algorithm based on our formulae outperforms commonly used algorithms for finding A-optimal allocations. When continuous factors or design regions get involved, we develop a ForLion algorithm to find A-optimal designs with mixed factors. Numerical studies on real-data experiments show that our algorithms can find highly efficient designs with reduced numbers of distinct experimental settings, which may save both experimental time and cost significantly. Along with a rounding-off algorithm that converts approximate allocations to exact ones, we demonstrate that A-optimal designs may provide more accurate parameter estimates than commonly used alternatives.

entry.title: A Unified Framework for Inference with General Missingness Patterns and Machine Learning Imputation

link.title: A Unified Framework for Inference with General Missingness Patterns and Machine Learning Imputation

entry.content: Predictions from machine learning (ML) models are increasingly used to impute missing data, but their naive use risks biased inference. Existing methods provide valid inference with ML imputations regardless of prediction quality to enhance efficiency, while they are limited to either simple missing data structures or a missing-completely-at-random assumption. We develop a novel framework for valid statistical inference in Z-estimation problems using ML imputations under a missing-at-random assumption and for general missingness patterns. The method stratifies data by distinct missingness patterns and constructs an estimator by aggregating pattern-specific observed and prediction information. Theoretically, we establish the asymptotic properties and globally optimal aggregation that guarantees efficiency dominance over weighted complete-case analyses (WCCA). Practically, the method affords simple implementations by leveraging existing WCCA software. Extensive simulations validate theoretical results and show clear competitiveness in various scenarios. An analysis of All of Us data further demonstrates the utility of the method. The paper concludes with a brief discussion on practical implications and potential future directions.

entry.title: Diff-Feat: Diffusion-Based Cross-Modal Feature Extraction for Multi-Label Classification

link.title: Diff-Feat: Diffusion-Based Cross-Modal Feature Extraction for Multi-Label Classification

entry.content: Multi-label classification has broad applications and depends on powerful representations capable of capturing multiple interactions. We introduce Diff-Feat, a simple yet effective framework that extracts intermediate features from pre-trained diffusion-Transformer models for both images and text, and fuses them for downstream tasks. We observe distinct patterns in optimal feature selection: for vision tasks, the most discriminative intermediate feature along the diffusion process occurs at the middle step and is located at the middle block in Transformer. In contrast, for language tasks, the best feature occurs at the noise-free step and is located at the deepest block. Notably, a consistent phenomenon across diverse datasets: a fixed “Middle Layer” yields the best performance on various downstream classification tasks for images (under DiT-XL/2-256$\times$256 and various U-ViT architectures). We further analyze the underlying mechanism and its scaling behavior across model scales. entry.title: Sliding-Window Signatures as Features for Time Series Forecasting

link.title: Sliding-Window Signatures as Features for Time Series Forecasting

entry.content: The evolution of a time series is often influenced not only by its past values but also by external covariates, giving rise to forecasting with exogenous variables. Nonlinear and delayed effects between covariates and the target series make this task particularly challenging. We propose a forecasting framework based on Ridge regression with sliding-window signature features, combining the computational efficiency of (semi-)parametric models with the flexibility of nonparametric approaches. These features capture complex dependencies between the target and the exogenous variables without relying on prior assumptions about the form of these relationships or the influence of past observations. We establish theoretical guarantees in the discrete-time setting, including universality of approximation and stationarity for the sliding-window transform. To ease implementation, we introduce a novel sequential algorithm that exploits window overlap for efficient signature updates. The method is evaluated on both synthetic and real electricity demand data. Results show that signature features effectively encode temporal and nonlinear dependencies, yielding accurate forecasts competitive with those based on expert knowledge and recent neural network approaches.

entry.title: Joint modeling and inference of multiple-subject high-dimensional sparse vector autoregressive models

link.title: Joint modeling and inference of multiple-subject high-dimensional sparse vector autoregressive models

entry.content: The multiple-subject vector autoregression (multi-VAR) model captures heterogeneous temporal dependence across subjects through commonly shared and subject-unique paths (entries) of individual (subject-specific) sparse VAR transition matrices. Available joint penalized regression approaches suffer from statistical inefficiency, whereby the convergence rates of the individual estimators are determined by a subject with the largest sparsity level. An enhanced multi-VAR estimation approach is proposed based on a communication-efficient data integration framework and a suitable identifiability condition in meta-analysis. It is shown that component-wise different convergence rates can be achieved. A hypothesis testing framework is also developed to assess the significance of common paths, as well as the homogeneity of subject-specific paths. Furthermore, a multiple hypothesis test to control the false discovery rate is suggested within a subregion of interest among the entire paths. A simulation study and a real data application compare the performance of the considered methods to other approaches.

link.title: Gini representations of skewness, kurtosis and higher-order moments

entry.content: We provide pairwise-difference (Gini-type) representations of higher-order central moments for both general random variables and empirical moments. Such representations do not require a measure of location. For third and fourth moments, this yields pairwise-difference representations of skewness and kurtosis coefficients. We show that all central moments possess such representations, so no reference to the mean is needed for moments of any order. This is done by considering i.i.d. replications of the random variables considered, by observing that central moments can be interpreted as covariances between a random variable and powers of the same variable, and by giving recursions which link the pairwise-difference representation of any moment to lower order ones.

link.title: Wasserstein-Cramér-Rao Theory of Unbiased Estimation

entry.content: The quantity of interest in the classical Cram'er-Rao theory of unbiased estimation (e.g., the Cram'er-Rao lower bound, its exact attainment for exponential families, and asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation) is the variance, which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an independently-sampled data set from the same distribution. In this paper we are interested in a quantity which represents the instability of an estimator when its value is compared to the value for an infinitesimal additive perturbation of the original data set; we refer to this as the “sensitivity” of an estimator. The resulting theory of sensitivity is based on the Wasserstein geometry in the same way that the classical theory of variance is based on the Fisher-Rao (equivalently, Hellinger) geometry, and this insight allows us to determine a collection of results which are analogous to the classical case: a Wasserstein-Cram'er-Rao lower bound for the sensitivity of any unbiased estimator, a characterization of models in which there exist unbiased estimators achieving the lower bound exactly, and various results on the asymptotic achievement of the lower bound. More precisely, we show that Wasserstein projection estimators (and one-step approximations thereof) are asymptotically sensitivity-efficient under suitable assumptions, and that there exist Hodges-type estimators which exhibit super-sensitivity-efficiency. We use these results to treat many statistical examples, sometimes revealing new optimality properties for existing estimators and other times revealing entirely new estimators.

entry.title: Group Competition Test: A P-value-free False Discovery Rate Control Framework for Grouped Hypotheses

link.title: Group Competition Test: A P-value-free False Discovery Rate Control Framework for Grouped Hypotheses

entry.content: Grouped multiple testing arises in many high-dimensional applications, where hypotheses may differ across groups and valid p-values are unavailable. Applying competition-based procedures separately within groups can inflate the global false discovery rate (FDR), while conservative corrections may substantially reduce power. We extend the competition test framework to the grouped setting and propose two procedures. The group competition (GC) test provides finite-sample FDR bounds under arbitrary inter-group dependence. For homogeneous groups, the required correction has logarithmic order in the number of groups, and this order is unavoidable for the GC test. The consistent group competition (CGC) filter instead couples group-specific thresholds through a single global normalization. Under the stated basic-independence conditions, it controls the FDR in finite samples without a correction that grows with the number of groups; under arbitrary inter-group dependence, the same guarantee is retained with a per-group correction that depends on the symmetry parameter of each group. We further develop a parameterized-threshold analysis to establish asymptotic guarantees and to characterize when the per-group correction can be dropped, so that a simple filter still controls the FDR approximately. Simulation studies show that the GC test and the CGC filter can improve power over pooled competition testing in heterogeneous settings, whereas the pooled test may remain more powerful under homogeneity. A peptide-spectrum matching benchmark involving post-translational modifications illustrates the practical relevance of the proposed methods.

entry.title: A Statistical Framework for Understanding Causal Effects that Vary by Treatment Initiation Time in EHR-based Studies

link.title: A Statistical Framework for Understanding Causal Effects that Vary by Treatment Initiation Time in EHR-based Studies

entry.content: Standard practice in electronic health record (EHR)-based studies evaluating the comparative effectiveness of bariatric surgery relative to no surgery is to estimate and report a constant treatment effect across calendar time. However, real-world treatment strategies can evolve, particularly when comparators include standard of care or surgical procedures where techniques may improve, making it clinically important to ascertain whether efficacy of bariatric surgery has changed over time. Efforts to determine whether treatment efficacy itself is evolving are complicated by changing patient populations, with potential covariate shift in key effect modifiers. Through a comprehensive analysis of EHR data from Kaiser Permanente comparing two bariatric surgical procedures to standard of care, we develop a statistical framework to estimate calendar time-specific average treatment effects and describe both how and why effects vary across treatment initiation time in EHR-based studies. Our approach projects doubly robust, time-specific treatment effect estimates onto candidate marginal structural models and uses model selection to best describe how effects vary by calendar time. We further introduce a novel summary metric, based on standardization, to quantify the degree to which observed effect changes may be attributed to covariate shift in the population receiving treatment, as opposed to changes in underlying treatment efficacy.

entry.title: Computationally efficient goodness-of-fit tests through kernelized Stein discrepancy

link.title: Computationally efficient goodness-of-fit tests through kernelized Stein discrepancy

entry.content: Models with intractable normalizing constants are widely used in statistics and machine learning. Assessing the adequacy of such models poses significant challenges: obtaining samples from the fitted model often requires sophisticated sampling algorithms. Moreover, model fitting sometimes requires iterative numerical optimization, making bootstrap procedures that require repeated refitting computationally expensive. In this paper, we leverage the kernel-based testing framework to develop a general semiparametric goodness-of-fit test based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy. We establish the consistency and the asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic under general nuisance estimation. To produce a level-$\alpha$ test, we propose a novel influence-adjusted wild bootstrap that requires neither refitting the model nor sampling from it. We prove the consistency of the proposed bootstrap test procedure under the null and the alternative, and characterize its limiting power under contiguous local alternatives. Across simulations ranging from classical normality testing to models with intractable likelihoods, the proposed test delivers competitive or superior power at a computational cost orders of magnitude lower than that of existing approaches. We illustrate the method by assessing the adequacy of a protein signaling network model for reverse-phase protein array data from lung adenocarcinoma tumors. As a complementary insight, we show that the SKSD test can be regarded as a nonparametric score test under exponentially tilted models, connecting score-based and distance-based goodness-of-fit testing.

entry.title: Reevaluating Causal Estimation Methods with Data from a Product Release

link.title: Reevaluating Causal Estimation Methods with Data from a Product Release

entry.content: Machine learning methods estimate flexible relationships between confounders, treatments and outcomes, making unconfoundedness assumptions in causal analysis more palatable. How successful are these approaches in recovering ground truth baselines? We analyze new data covering an experimental rollout of a software product feature for one group of users and a voluntary opt-in to the same feature for another similar group. Recovering causal effects from nonrandomized data is feasible–but only with careful modeling choices. We offer best practices for more credible treatment effect estimation in modern, high-dimensional datasets and evaluate which tests provide meaningful signals about the reliability of estimated effects.

entry.title: Multi-Domain Empirical Bayes for Linearly-Mixed Causal Representations

link.title: Multi-Domain Empirical Bayes for Linearly-Mixed Causal Representations

entry.content: Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to learn low-dimensional causal latent variables from high-dimensional observations. While identifiability has been extensively studied for CRL, estimation has been less explored. We use empirical Bayes (EB) to estimate causal representations from multiple domains whose differences reflect interventions in a shared causal model. Multi-domain CRL poses a simultaneous inference problem suited to EB. Here, we propose an EB $f$-modeling algorithm that improves the quality of learned causal variables by exploiting invariant structure within and across domains. Specifically, we consider linear measurement models with interventional priors induced by an acyclic latent causal model with known graph and intervention targets. We develop an EM-style algorithm based on causally structured score matching. In experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic single-cell data, our proposed method achieves more accurate estimation than alternative methods and baselines.

link.title: A new gradient-free active subspace estimation method with application to rare event probability estimation

entry.content: To reduce the cost of estimating the probability of a rare event involving a very large number of random parameters, we propose a new strategy for dimension reduction coupled with a surrogate model for the expensive part of the algorithm. To this end, we extend the Ordinary Kriging Active Subspace (OK-AS) method into a sequential version. Our approach consists of iteratively re-estimating the active subspace using a Kriging surrogate trained in a rotated coordinate system until the active subspace stabilises. This method allows for a reduction in prediction error and a better approximation of the active subspace on a benchmark of test problems. Furthermore, we integrate our algorithm into an efficient pre-existing approach for estimating the probability of a rare event. This approach is based on learning the active subspace associated with the random event whose probability is to be estimated. The sequential learning of an importance sampling density is necessary and corresponds to the expensive part of this strategy. To circumvent this issue, we integrate our sequential OK-AS version into the estimation of the importance sampling density. The numerical results indicate that our method allows for reducing the cost required to obtain a precise estimate of the rare event probability.

entry.title: Lumbermark: Resistant Clustering by Chopping Up Mutual Reachability Minimum Spanning Trees

link.title: Lumbermark: Resistant Clustering by Chopping Up Mutual Reachability Minimum Spanning Trees

entry.content: We introduce Lumbermark, a robust divisive clustering algorithm capable of detecting clusters of varying sizes, densities, and shapes. Lumbermark iteratively chops off large limbs connected by protruding segments of a dataset’s mutual reachability minimum spanning tree. The use of mutual reachability distances smoothens the data distribution and decreases the influence of low-density objects, such as noise points between clusters or outliers at their peripheries. The algorithm can be viewed as a divisive version of Genie and an alternative to HDBSCAN that produces partitions with user-specified sizes. A fast, easy-to-use implementation of this new method is available in the open-source lumbermark package for Python and R. We show that Lumbermark performs well on benchmark data and hope it will prove useful to data scientists and practitioners across different fields.

entry.title: Iterative Identification Closure: Amplifying Causal Identifiability in Linear SEMs

link.title: Iterative Identification Closure: Amplifying Causal Identifiability in Linear SEMs

entry.content: The Half-Trek Criterion (HTC) is the primary graphical tool for determining generic identifiability of causal effect coefficients in linear structural equation models (SEMs) with latent confounders. However, HTC is inherently node-wise: it simultaneously resolves all incoming edges of a node, leaving a gap of “inconclusive” causal effects (15-23% in moderate graphs). We introduce Iterative Identification Closure (IIC), a general framework that decouples causal identification into two phases: (1) a seed function S_0 that identifies an initial set of edges from any external source of information (instrumental variables, interventions, non-Gaussianity, prior knowledge, etc.); and (2) Reduced HTC propagation that iteratively substitutes known coefficients to reduce system dimension, enabling identification of edges that standard HTC cannot resolve. The core novelty is iterative identification propagation: newly identified edges feed back to unlock further identification – a mechanism absent from all existing graphical criteria, which treat each edge (or node) in isolation. This propagation is non-trivial: coefficient substitution alters the covariance structure, and soundness requires proving that the modified Jacobian retains generic full rank – a new theoretical result (Reduced HTC Theorem). We prove that IIC is sound, monotone, converges in O( E ) iterations (empirically <=2), and strictly subsumes both HTC and ancestor decomposition. Exhaustive verification on all graphs with n<=5 (134,144 edges) confirms 100% precision (zero false positives); with combined seeds, IIC reduces the HTC gap by over 80%. The propagation gain is gamma~4x (2 seeds identifying ~3% of edges to 97.5% total identification), far exceeding gamma<=1.2x of prior methods that incorporate side information without iterative feedback.

entry.title: SENECA: Small-Sample Discrete Entropy Estimation via Self-Consistent Missing Mass

link.title: SENECA: Small-Sample Discrete Entropy Estimation via Self-Consistent Missing Mass

entry.content: Discrete entropy estimation is a classic information theory problem, wherein the average information content of a discrete random variable is estimated from samples alone. Naive approaches, such as the plugin method, fail to account for the probability mass associated with members of the random variable’s support that are unobserved in a given sample, known as the “missing mass.” The resulting systemic underestimation is particularly problematic when data is time-consuming or costly to gather. We propose SENECA, an entropy estimation scheme based on a novel “self-consistent” missing mass calculation. Extensive numerical experiments indicate that our approach outperforms many state-of-the-art alternatives overall in the small-sample setting. We then apply SENECA to two practical use cases, namely biodiversity estimation and the detection of incorrect large language model responses, where our method is competitive with domain-specific approaches. Our work advances SENECA as an effective drop-in replacement for small-sample entropy estimation, with broad utility across several domains.

entry.title: Isotonic Conformal Inference

link.title: Isotonic Conformal Inference

entry.content: A predictor with small overall bias can still exhibit systematic bias conditional on its predicted value, limiting its reliability for downstream uncertainty quantification and candidate screening. We propose Isotonic Conformal Inference, a unified framework for prediction and multiple testing that separates calibration from inference and exploits the level set structure of an isotonic predictor. This structure enables the computation of localized conformal quantiles and $p$-values while avoiding repeated isotonic refitting across candidate responses. For prediction, we introduce Split Isotonic Conformal Prediction (sICP) and Transductive Isotonic Conformal Prediction (tICP), establish prediction-conditional coverage guarantees for both methods, and characterize their finite-sample and asymptotic self-calibration properties. For selection, we introduce Isotonic Conformal Selection (ICS), which provides finite-sample stratum-conditional false discovery rate control. Experiments on simulated regression problems, a healthcare-utilization dataset, and a high-throughput ADMET drug discovery dataset demonstrate the practical performance of the framework and substantially lower computational costs relative to full transductive baselines.

entry.title: High-Dimensional Change Point Analysis for Temporally Dependent Data

link.title: High-Dimensional Change Point Analysis for Temporally Dependent Data

entry.content: This paper develops adaptive procedures for detecting and locating mean changes in high-dimensional time series. Quadratic CUSUM statistics target dense changes, whereas coordinatewise maximum statistics target sparse changes. Two weighting schemes are considered to accommodate both interior and boundary changes. Under general non-Gaussian vector dependence, we establish the limiting distributions, validate the required centering and scaling estimators, and prove asymptotic independence between matched quadratic and maximum statistics. These results justify Cauchy combination tests. We further establish single-change localization and consistent multiple-change recovery using wild binary segmentation. Numerical results illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

entry.title: SAKI-RoPE: Score-Aware Low-Rank Key Indexing with RoPE-Aware Covariance and Random-Matrix Noise Analysis

link.title: SAKI-RoPE: Score-Aware Low-Rank Key Indexing with RoPE-Aware Covariance and Random-Matrix Noise Analysis

entry.content: Existing low-rank KV-cache indexes preserve model weights or key variance, not the attention scores that determine retrieval. We derive the expected score distortion of key-side rank-r compression, a two-sided covariance-weighted low-rank problem that uses both query and key statistics, and solve it exactly: the optimum is an optimal rank-r linear score map, computed in closed form from two d x d covariances per head, and its predicted per-head score-MSE reduction matches measurement (Pearson r = 0.997). The resulting training-free index, SAKI, beats key-PCA at every rank on LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.2-3B, at every context length from 4K to 64K, and in every calibration-domain pair (0.748 -> 0.799 recall@64 at r = 32 on LLaMA-3.1-8B). Because RoPE rotates keys by their distance from the query, we make the closed form RoPE-aware by averaging the query covariance over rotations; this SAKI-RoPE, our main method, raises recall to 0.861, beats PCA on every head of all four models, and needs only 28-39% of PCA’s rank to match it at r = 32 across the four models. Random-matrix theory of the covariance estimation noise shows that 512 calibration tokens suffice and that clipping the Marchenko-Pastur noise bulk helps SAKI when calibration is short. We make no perplexity claim: with the attention sink pinned, perplexity differences between indexes are small and depend on model and text, and we show that any low-rank index calibrated on a long prefix drops the attention-sink token, which collapses 32K perplexity unless the sink is pinned.

entry.title: Ultra-high-dimensional spot support screening in continuous-time regression

link.title: Ultra-high-dimensional spot support screening in continuous-time regression

entry.content: We study variable screening for high-frequency continuous-time regression, targeting the support of the spot regression coefficient. Under coordinatewise truncation and finite-variation jumps, uniform entrywise bounds for local correlation estimates yield the rate ${(\log p)/n}^{\alpha/(2\alpha+1)}$ under a local averaged $\alpha$-H"older condition, up to confidence and grid factors. These bounds imply sure screening for the marginal support. To retain the regression support under local dependence, we propose partial-residual spot iterative screening with pathwise Lepski adaptation. Under sparse eigenvalues and standardized beta-min, the procedure has the sure screening property and requires only correlation columns associated with the current active set. A list-size minimax lower bound applies to both support targets and matches the localization and multiplicity order of the marginal-screening bound when $\log(p/d)\asymp\log p$. Simulations and a high-frequency factor application illustrate the procedures.

entry.title: Bias-robust causal inference for panel data

link.title: Bias-robust causal inference for panel data

entry.content: We develop a bias-robust framework for causal inference in panel data models with interactive fixed effects. Conventional imputation-based estimators of average treatment effects on the treated do not explicitly account for counterfactual approximation error, potentially leading to misleading inference. Building on bias-aware minimax methods, we construct an estimator that corrects imputed counterfactuals using weighted untreated residuals and delivers confidence intervals with an explicit allowance for the remaining approximation bias. The resulting framework separates protection against approximation bias from the efficiency gains obtained through optimal correction. In simulations, the correction reduces confidence interval length by approximately 13\% relative to bias-aware inference without correction, while preserving empirical coverage. An application to Election Day Registration demonstrates how the correction strengthens the robustness of substantive conclusions to counterfactual error. The proposed approach provides a transparent sensitivity analysis for causal effects when the accuracy of counterfactual imputation cannot be established from observed data alone.

entry.title: Bayesian Generalized Network Autoregressive Model with Structured Shrinkage and Persistence Priors

link.title: Bayesian Generalized Network Autoregressive Model with Structured Shrinkage and Persistence Priors

entry.content: We propose a Bayesian generalized network autoregressive (BGNAR) model for multivariate time series whose component series are associated with the nodes of a known network. The proposed framework combines the parsimonious network structure of the generalized network autoregressive (GNAR) model with structured shrinkage and persistence priors adapted from Bayesian vector autoregressive (BVAR) modeling. We adapt Minnesota-type shrinkage to both own-lag and network-lag coefficients, with prior variances decreasing over temporal lags and, for network effects, neighborhood orders. A hierarchical prior on the own-lag coefficients allows information to be shared across nodes while retaining node-specific heterogeneity. We further adapt the sum-of-coefficients and dummy-initial-observation priors to the GNAR parameterization. Posterior inference is performed using a Gibbs sampler. Simulation studies show that BGNAR can use the same deliberately over-specified temporal and neighborhood structure across datasets without dataset-specific BIC order selection, while maintaining forecasting accuracy comparable to BIC-selected GNAR and outperforming the unrestricted BVAR benchmark in the settings considered. The structured prior regularizes weakly supported coefficients toward zero within this fixed model. Posterior distributions for the dynamic coefficients and posterior predictive distributions for future observations provide direct quantification of parameter and predictive uncertainty. An application to a wind-speed network demonstrates that BGNAR achieves point-forecast performance comparable to GNAR while additionally providing posterior inference on own-lag and network-lag effects and posterior predictive uncertainty.

entry.title: Multisource Remote Sensing and Geospatial Analysis of Vineyard Wildfire Impacts and Exposure: The 2019 Kincade Fire

link.title: Multisource Remote Sensing and Geospatial Analysis of Vineyard Wildfire Impacts and Exposure: The 2019 Kincade Fire

entry.content: Working agricultural landscapes are often treated as background to wildfire disasters, even though they are managed fuel mosaics, productive assets, and parts of regional infrastructure systems. We examine vineyard wildfire resilience during the electrically initiated 2019 Kincade Fire in Sonoma County, California, using an open, event-anchored geospatial framework spanning 4,581 vineyard fields (8,813.2 ha), wildland vegetation, surveyed structures, roads, overhead smoke, and post-fire greenness. Sentinel-2, OpenET, gridMET, soils, terrain, NOAA smoke polygons, an ignition-date OpenStreetMap network, and three-dimensional data inventories were analyzed at native decision scales. Vineyard pixels showed substantially lower descriptive dNBR than wildland pixels inside the perimeter (means 0.130 and 0.337). This contrast did not identify a universal vineyard firebreak effect: a segment-clustered boundary model gave a small negative contrast at 100 m (tau = -0.0166) but changed across bandwidths, failed slope continuity, disappeared in a 100 m donut, and produced a wrong-signed placebo. A 250 m spatial GAM reversed the unconditional pattern: after conditioning on location, terrain, and water use, vineyard fraction was positively associated with dNBR, while residual Moran’s I remained 0.519. Beyond spectral impact, all mapped vineyards intersected overhead smoke on at least one day (mean 7.78 potential smoke-days per field), 34.2% of road-network nodes were dead ends, and inside-perimeter vineyards showed a larger greenness deficit through 2021 (recovery ratios 0.815 inside and 0.854 outside). Lower immediate spectral impact therefore did not imply complete resilience. The study provides a reproducible urban-rural informatics template separating descriptive contrasts, conditional associations, exposure indicators, and recovery evidence for decisions in working landscapes.

entry.title: Statistical Inference for Bivariate Functional Causal Discovery

link.title: Statistical Inference for Bivariate Functional Causal Discovery

entry.content: Causal discovery methods aim to determine the causal direction between variables using observational data. Functional causal discovery methods rely on structural and distributional assumptions to determine directionality but typically lack statistical inference. This paper reviews the statistical guarantees of existing functional causal discovery methods in theory, software, and applied use, highlighting a key gap: the absence of a unified inferential framework that applies broadly across model classes. As a first step toward addressing this gap, we formalize a test-based approach for bivariate causal discovery by repurposing goodness-of-fit and independence tests within a hypothesis-testing framework. Because directionality is determined through two disjoint hypothesis tests, corresponding to four causal discovery outcomes, the approach provides explicit uncertainty quantification and diagnostic insight into assumption violations. Resampling is further used to estimate the rates of causal discovery outcomes, offering an additional layer of inference. We demonstrate the use and behavior of our inferential framework through simulations that vary the degree of assumption violation, as well as through real-data applications. We conclude with practical lessons and recommendations for advancing statistical guarantees in functional causal discovery.

entry.title: Projected Effects of Naloxone and Buprenorphine Scale-Up on Opioid Overdose Mortality in Six Pennsylvania Counties

link.title: Projected Effects of Naloxone and Buprenorphine Scale-Up on Opioid Overdose Mortality in Six Pennsylvania Counties

entry.content: Opioid overdose deaths remain a severe public health crisis in the US, with heterogeneous burden across counties that differ in epidemic trajectory, baseline resources, and local context. While harm reduction through naloxone distribution and buprenorphine treatment are both evidence-based strategies, limited information on county-level effects hinders the ability of policymakers to prioritize resources across counties. We developed a simulation model of opioid use disorder (OUD), calibrated separately to six Pennsylvania counties spanning large urban (Allegheny, Philadelphia), intermediate-sized (Erie, Dauphin), and rural (Clearfield, Columbia) settings. We projected county-specific overdose mortality trajectories under three levels of increase in buprenorphine dispensing and naloxone distribution (10%, 20%, and 30% above each county’s baseline), over a five-year horizon from 2025 to 2029. A 30% increase in naloxone distribution above projected county baseline levels was projected to reduce 2029 overdose deaths by approximately 70% (95% uncertainty interval, UI: 55-81%) in Allegheny County, 11% (95% UI: 4-17%) in Erie County, and 28% (95% UI: 2-64%) in Clearfield County. The relative projected benefits of naloxone and buprenorphine varied by county; buprenorphine produced larger reductions in Erie and Dauphin. The same proportional increase in naloxone distribution produced substantially different projected mortality reductions across the six Pennsylvania counties. County-level context is important for informing harm reduction and treatment prioritization at the county level.

entry.title: The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures

link.title: The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures

entry.content: Many statistical procedures compute an entire solution path rather than a single estimator. For one class the path is piecewise linear, traced corner to corner by an active-set homotopy. Two of its members coincide exactly: under $\Sigma=X^\top X$ and $\mu=X^\top y$ the gross-exposure-constrained mean–variance program and the constrained LASSO trace the same piecewise-linear curve, and they keep doing so under arbitrary linear equality and inequality constraints. Which parameter is swept, a leverage budget or a return tilt, is not a choice the curve notices: under a homogeneous mandate the two sweeps differ by a scalar. A mandate that holds the portfolio invested costs a radial rescaling instead, and the efficient frontier is that curve rescaled; its corners pass unnoticed because the frontier is continuously differentiable where they fall. We give the map between the two parametrisations and the single way it degenerates. That mean–variance selection and the LASSO instantiate one parametric quadratic program is prior art (G"artner, Jaggi and Maria, 2012). The Critical Line Algorithm itself lies off that route, and the correspondence established here is new. The identity is one of curves, not of statistical experiments. The map between the parametrisations is computed from the data, so the geometry of the path transfers while quantities averaged over the response do not. We cross that boundary deliberately and give the degrees of freedom of the constrained fit under arbitrary linear constraints. In the long-only, fully invested case it is the expected number of holdings away from a bound, less one.

entry.title: Discussion on “Principled type I error rate inflation in two-arm clinical trial designs with external control information borrowing” by Silvia Calderazzo, Manuel Wiesenfarth, Vivienn Weru, and Annette Kopp-Schneider

link.title: Discussion on “Principled type I error rate inflation in two-arm clinical trial designs with external control information borrowing” by Silvia Calderazzo, Manuel Wiesenfarth, Vivienn Weru, and Annette Kopp-Schneider

entry.content: Consideration of frequentist type-I error or power based on certain fixed conditions may not fully embrace the aims of a Bayesian analysis; this is particularly true in settings where informative priors are involved. Calderazzo et al. consider adaptations of a testing procedure involving Bayesian borrowing from external control data. Particular caution may be necessary here in order not to condition on parameters and data simultaneously. We consider their example case and argue that (a) the conditioning scheme may have limited practical implications, and (b) if the main concern are assumption violations, these might be better addressed by adapting the likelihood function.

entry.title: Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partially observed Time Series (LIFTS)

link.title: Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partially observed Time Series (LIFTS)

entry.content: Partially observed multivariate time series pose two coupled challenges: recovering missing measurements and forecasting future trajectories when observation patterns are informative. Existing methods often assume ignorable missingness or use the mask only as an auxiliary input. We propose LIFTS (Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partly observed Time Series), a probabilistic framework in which a latent process jointly governs the complete measurement trajectory and observation mask, allowing observation patterns to inform latent-state inference for both forecasting and imputation. LIFTS combines flexible neural-network parameterizations with a forward-backward architecture: the forward pass performs filtering and autoregressive forecasting, while the backward pass performs smoothing and conditional multiple imputation. The model and inference components are trained jointly using a masked energy score and self-masking. We establish forward-backward distributional representations for the general framework and, for an explicit structural subclass, provide full-law identification and consistency guarantees. Simulations and an application to PhysioNet 2019 show that LIFTS provides accurate point predictions, improved distributional accuracy, and well-calibrated predictive intervals; it outperforms competing methods particularly when training data are limited and has substantially faster inference than the diffusion-based baseline.

entry.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

link.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

entry.content: Mortgage credit risk may exhibit dependence across economically connected areas, even when they are geographically distant. However, current models typically represent cross-area dependence through fixed geographical neighbourhoods, potentially overlooking economic connections that extend beyond physical proximity and evolve over time. These models may fail to capture shared risks among geographically distant but economically similar areas, and cannot describe a changing dependence of risk; it therefore risks retaining economically obsolete connections while omitting newly emerging ones. This paper uses similarities of industrial composition as a measure of economic proximity and develops a discrete-time survival model with dynamic industrial graphs to capture evolving cross-area dependence in mortgage default risk. The resulting graphs are reconstructed annually, allowing both their topology and edge weights to change as regional industrial compositions evolve. Jointly combining a proper conditional autoregressive process with a first-order autoregressive process governs the temporal cross-area dependence and the temporal persistence in latent risk simultaneously. The model is estimated using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation and evaluated on U.S. mortgage loan-level data against the static industrial graph specifications. The results show that the proposed dynamic model achieves better in-sample fit and out-of-sample discrimination, while its estimated parameters indicate substantial graph-induced cross-area dependence and temporal persistence. These findings demonstrate the value of allowing economically defined neighbourhoods to evolve when modelling mortgage default risk.

entry.title: Analytically Optimal Sample Allocations for Nested Multivariate Multifidelity Control Variate Estimators

link.title: Analytically Optimal Sample Allocations for Nested Multivariate Multifidelity Control Variate Estimators

entry.content: Monte Carlo estimation, an essential tool for quantifying uncertainty in complex scientific and engineering applications, often has unacceptably large errors when computing resources are limited and each sample requires evaluating an expensive high-fidelity model. Multifidelity control variate methods seek to increase the accuracy of Monte Carlo estimation by combining a limited number of expensive high-fidelity samples with a larger number of cheaper lower-fidelity samples. Many different multifidelity estimators have been proposed, including multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC), multifidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC), approximate control variates (ACVs), and multilevel best linear unbiased estimators (MLBLUEs). An important design choice in multifidelity estimation is the allocation of a limited computational budget among the available models to minimize estimator error. The state of the art in solving this budget allocation problem relies on numerical optimization; to date, closed form solutions have only been derived for estimator forms known to be suboptimal. In this work, we provide closed form expressions for optimal fractional sample allocations for a large class of nested multifidelity control variate estimators, in which higher-fidelity models are evaluated on a subset of the inputs that lower-fidelity models are evaluated on. Our analysis is based on reformulating nested MLBLUEs as an extended version of the MFMC estimator, and is applicable to general multivariate Monte Carlo estimation. We additionally propose a new approach for integer-valued budget allocation based on a greedy strategy used in combinatorial optimization, as well as a method for robust approximation of control variate coefficients from limited pilot samples. Two numerical examples illustrate our theoretical results and demonstrate the increased accuracy of our extended MFMC formulation relative to existing estimators.

entry.title: Persistence is not Independence: A structural Credibility Protocol for Distribution based Recovery in VARLiNGAM

link.title: Persistence is not Independence: A structural Credibility Protocol for Distribution based Recovery in VARLiNGAM

entry.content: VAR-LiNGAM recovers a contemporaneous structure from reduced-form innovations under mutual independence of the underlying structural shocks. Recovery itself and bootstrap stability of the recovered edges are natural post-estimation outputs, but neither directly assesses the identifying independence assumption. We organize post-recovery validation as an ordered, non-compensatory protocol with four layers (reduced-form admissibility, distributional informativeness, independence support and edge persistence) and establish, by a constructive population result, a Monte Carlo experiment under known ground truth and a firm-level Compustat application, that the last two layers are non-nested: an edge can persist under resampling while the recovered shocks remain dependent, and independence can be supported while the leading recovered edge fails to persist. Independence support is classified operationally by a block-permutation dHSIC diagnostic on the recovered shocks, with mutual information as a continuous measure of residual dependence and tail co-exceedance as a complementary extreme-dependence diagnostic. Empirically, the conjunction of no detected independence violation and a reportable persistent leading edge occurs only in a small subset.

entry.title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release

link.title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release

entry.content: Computational gene-function prediction generates annotations at a scale that experimental characterization cannot match, yet substantial errors remain even among leading methods. Explicit error-controlled calibration for Gene Ontology (GO) prediction remains largely undeveloped. We introduce GoCo, a structure-guided framework that calibrates how scores from an existing predictor are converted into released annotations. GoCo certifies a global threshold for a GO-hierarchy-aware gene-level false discovery proportion (FDP), then constructs a nested release path under the same asymptotic risk-control guarantee. At the primary operating point (alpha=0.10, delta=0.50), GoCo-M, developed on Wainberg co-essentiality modules and applied without retuning to three independent studies with the same shared-evidence structure, kept mean held-out gene-level FDP at or below target while releasing 6.3-17.6% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel. For gene-specific neighbourhoods, GoCo-N orders individual calls. Developed on FunMap and validated without retuning on the STRING v12.0 experiments-only network, GoCo-N released 33.8% and 36.4% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel on the same refined score grid in FunMap and STRING, respectively, while keeping mean held-out FDP below target. The same pattern held under the stricter delta=0.10 setting. Thus, predictor-native biological structure can be reused at calibration, not only prediction, to release more supported annotations at a chosen gene-level error target without retraining the predictor.

entry.title: TGAge: A Phenotypic Aging Clock Based on Tabular Foundation Models and the Gompertz Law for Assisted Living Facility Residents

link.title: TGAge: A Phenotypic Aging Clock Based on Tabular Foundation Models and the Gompertz Law for Assisted Living Facility Residents

entry.content: Biological age captures overall health status beyond chronological age, yet existing biological aging clocks are difficult to apply to assisted living facility (ALF) residents due to scarce epigenetic data. We propose TGAge, a second-generation phenotypic aging clock that estimates risk-equivalent biological age from routinely collected clinical measurements. TGAge employs a tabular foundation model to predict all-cause mortality risks over discrete time-to-death intervals and converts the resulting mortality-risk ratio into biological age acceleration via the Gompertz law. We develop and evaluate TGAge on a large cohort of ALF residents curated from a proprietary, multi-state long-term care database. TGAge outperforms clinical indices and established biological aging clocks in survival prediction. Moreover, TGAge-derived age acceleration is significantly associated with multiple aging-related comorbidities. These findings support TGAge as a practical, interpretable, and highly predictive biological aging clock for vulnerable ALF populations using only routinely collected clinical measurements.

entry.title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data

link.title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data

entry.content: Researchers often pool public gut microbiome datasets from immunotherapy studies to get around small sample sizes, assuming that adding cohorts adds statistical power faster than it adds differences between studies. We test that assumption. We processed four public shotgun metagenomic cohorts of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade through one pipeline and pooled them step by step, from 39 to 283 patients. Because the PERMANOVA effect size R^2 is above zero even when there is no real effect, we compared every result with its exact chance expectation. Measured as raw variance explained, cohort membership accounted for 8 to 27 times more variance than treatment response, although much of that ratio comes from sample size alone. At every pooling step, treatment response explained no more variance than chance (within 0.2 percentage points) and was never significant, while cohort membership explained 6.0 to 9.5 percentage points beyond chance (p = 0.001 each time). Classification stayed at chance across three model types, none of six leak-free batch-correction strategies recovered signal, and no genus reached significance in a random-effects meta-analysis. The largest single cohort (n = 165) was also non-significant, although simulation shows it had at least 90% power to detect an effect at its own 95% upper bound; within it, recruiting site alone explained 7.0 percentage points beyond chance. In three tumor genomic cohorts (n = 223), a small but real response effect sat next to a cohort effect about eighteen times larger, so the problem is not specific to microbiome data. We release batch_detector, an open tool that reports chance-corrected cohort and response effects before pooling, and test it on an independent colorectal cancer meta-analysis.

entry.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mechanical Engineering: Foundations, Opportunities, Challenges, and Responsibilities

link.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mechanical Engineering: Foundations, Opportunities, Challenges, and Responsibilities

entry.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mechanical engineering (ME), from modeling, simulation, and optimization to diagnostics, design, and technical communication. Drawing on a round-table at the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering (COBEM 2025), this article presents a structured perspective for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than an exhaustive survey, it examines how AI can enhance engineering practice without compromising scientific rigor. We distinguish statistical learning from human cognition and discuss the capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic forms of AI. We then consider industrial adoption, workforce changes, and AI-assisted scientific discovery, alongside the energy and infrastructure demands of AI computation and their implications for sustainability and thermal management. The discussion emphasizes the integration of physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems, particularly in safety-relevant applications. Topics include physics-informed and hybrid learning, physically constrained modeling, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification. We also examine educational, epistemological, and ethical challenges, including curriculum reform, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the preservation of engineering knowledge. We conclude with principles for responsible AI adoption in ME: physical consistency, rigorous validation, explicit treatment of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. AI should complement, not replace, engineering judgment.

entry.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities

link.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities

entry.content: We generalize cubic smoothing splines to signals with a finite number of discontinuities at unknown positions. Rather than changing the roughness penalty, we deform the domain over which it is computed: every interval between consecutive observations can be stretched by a non-negative warp, subject to a total budget, and the optimizer spends the budget only where a jump makes stretching cheaper than bending. The estimator inherits the state-space form of smoothing splines, so it can be fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that solves a banded linear system and takes a projected-gradient step on the warps. The budget is selected by an extended Bayesian information criterion whose constant is calibrated by simulation. In a Monte Carlo comparison the new estimators reconstruct a piecewise-smooth signal more accurately than the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities of Storath and Weinmann, at the cost of more false alarms. Two energy applications illustrate the method: the temperature response of electricity demand in Northern Italy, and retail fuel prices, whose discontinuities, changes in excise duties, are dated by public record. The three supplements follow the references.

entry.title: Derivative-Informed Dimension Reduction of Stochastic Differential Equations: A Path-Space Sensitivity Approach

link.title: Derivative-Informed Dimension Reduction of Stochastic Differential Equations: A Path-Space Sensitivity Approach

entry.content: Uncertainty in the drift of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) induces uncertainty in statistical observables defined as expected functionals on path space. We propose a derivative-informed method for identifying low-dimensional structure in the drift-to-observable map, with the aim of improving the tractability of uncertainty quantification. This approach can be viewed as a generalization of the active subspace method to infinite-dimensional input spaces and to path-space observables of SDEs. Representing uncertainty in the drift by random perturbations in a Hilbert space, we construct a path-space sensitivity operator using first-order Fr'echet derivatives of the observable with respect to the perturbation. We establish conditions under which the leading eigenfunctions of this operator correspond to directions of maximum mean squared sensitivity of the observable, thus enabling low-dimensional approximation with certified error bounds. We further introduce a martingale control variate of the Fr'echet derivative that reduces error in sample-based estimators of the operator. Using a Galerkin scheme for numerical discretization, we show that reduced representations of the drift from the derivative-informed basis yield more accurate approximations of mean first hitting times of SDEs than the Karhunen-Lo`eve expansion of the same truncation order.

entry.title: Self-thresholding angular-radial models of extremal dependence

link.title: Self-thresholding angular-radial models of extremal dependence

entry.content: Assessing compound risks requires a model for routine and extreme joint behaviour together, and a principled answer to where the joint tail begins. We propose the self-thresholding angular-radial (STAR) model: after marginal standardization, the radius given the angle follows a spliced distribution, with a flexible body below an angle-dependent threshold curve and a generalized Pareto tail above it. The threshold curve is estimated with all other parameters, so its uncertainty propagates to every summary, and the joint density is in closed form because the splice normalizes in one dimension for every angle. The tail scale function is the reciprocal gauge of the implied limit set, and the coefficient of extremal association is an explicit parameter, so a prior with atoms at tail independence and at the asymptotic dependence boundary yields posterior probabilities of the dependence class. At that boundary the copula of the model is asymptotically dependent, while its margins and joint tail are both lighter than exponential by a factor inversely proportional to the level. Simulations show accurate recovery of finite-level dependence summaries within and beyond the model class, and the slow separation of asymptotic dependence from strong asymptotic independence that the theory predicts. For warm-season daily maxima of fine particulate matter and ozone at a Beijing station, the pair is asymptotically independent with posterior probability 0.96 and both pollutants exceed their 0.9 quantiles on about two and a half days per season; the model gives summaries comparable to those of existing approaches without requiring the arbitrary choice of a threshold. The construction extends to d dimensions through pairwise deficits of the gauge, illustrated by adding coarse particulate matter as a third pollutant.

entry.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables

link.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables

entry.content: Policy decisions often depend on whether the average treatment effect (ATE) exceeds a specific cutoff. In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the ATE requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify. Therefore, many researchers shift their attention to identification of the local (L) ATE or target bounds of the ATE. Both strategies have well-known drawbacks: the substantive relevance of the LATE is frequently questioned, and the bounds are often too wide to be informative. We propose a simple sensitivity analysis that allows researchers to maintain focus on the ATE, and then discuss its connection to related bounding procedures. Based on these results, researchers can decide, in a principled manner, whether the sign of the ATE is inferable under assumptions they deem credible. The proposed strategies are easy to apply, and we illustrate their value with two real-data examples. The R package ivate implements our procedures.
